claims.text: Mechanical-performance differences among FCC equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets are primarily governed by local lattice distortion.
The quinary alloy has greater atomic-radius diversity and larger misfit strains than its reduced-component subsets.
Misfit strain fields act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
The larger misfit strains in the quinary alloy promote deformation modes such as twinning.
Reducing the constituent count from five to four or three lowers local lattice distortion and its strengthening contribution.
The alloys can be compared after identical thermomechanical processing to obtain comparable microstructural states.
Atomic-size mismatch produces heterogeneous lattice-strain fields in the quinary alloy.
Heterogeneous lattice-strain fields impede dislocation propagation and increase yield strength.
Atomic-size mismatch encourages twinning and cross-slip.
Alloys with fewer elements have more uniform atomic spacing and fewer misfit-induced obstacles.
Relative to the quinary baseline, quaternary and ternary subsets will exhibit lower measured local lattice strain.
Lower local lattice strain in the quaternary and ternary subsets will be accompanied by lower strength and altered work-hardening rates.
The quinary alloy will have higher yield strength and more pronounced strain hardening than the quaternary and ternary subsets.
The proposed relationship is limited to single-phase FCC alloys dominated by dislocation glide and twinning.
The proposed relationship may not apply to alloys containing secondary phases or having non-FCC structures.
Existing evidence supports a link between lattice distortion and strength in high-entropy alloys.
Short-range order and electronic effects may also contribute to the mechanical-property differences.
